#6340. A honey bee’s stinger keeps pumping venom after the bee flies off, and now scientists know how

Video shows that a honey bee stinger works as a tiny, double-piston pump, with collapsing valves that keep pushing venom after the bee has gone.

A honey bee stings once, leaves its stinger in your skin, and flies off to die. It looks like the end of the attack. It isn’t.

The stinger left behind is a self-contained unit, with its own venom sac, muscles and nerves. It keeps digging in and pumping venom on its own after the bee has gone.

Scientists have now filmed that happening at high speed. Fiorella Ramirez-Esquivel of Macquarie University in Sydney and her colleagues watched detached stingers push into a clear gel that stands in for skin. The gel is not living tissue, but it lets a camera see what skin would hide.

The stinger, they found, works as a pump but is unlike most pumps that people build: two flexible pistons sliding in opposite directions inside a single chamber.

“We’ve known since as early as 1910 that the venom sac of a honey bee stinger empties into a chamber with little pumping elements called valves, but until now we didn’t know exactly how they work,” said Ramirez-Esquivel.

The honey bee is one of only a handful of insects whose stinger is built to tear away from its body. When the bee pulls free, the stinger stays put, along with its venom sac, several glands, a cluster of nerve cells, and the muscles that drive it.

The team, from Macquarie and UNSW Canberra, took stingers from live worker bees. Each tip went into a small block of clear gel about a sixth of an inch (4 millimeters) long.

A stinger is partly see-through, so a strong light shone through it let cameras running at up to 500 frames a second record the parts moving inside.

The stinger only pumped properly when it had something to push into. Without gel, its pumping parts barely moved. In the gel, strong pumping lasted from 15 seconds to just over a minute in a sample of 10 stingers.

It then faded to twitches that went on for two to five additional minutes. In an interview with Earth.com, Ramirez-Esquivel said the speed of the stinging made it hard to film.

“There is no time to adjust, you either catch it or you don’t,” she said. “I still did not expect the sheer number of attempts we had to go through to capture this footage.”

Inside the stinger, the venom sac empties into a small chamber at the base. Two long, sharp blades called lancets slide back and forth through that chamber along a rail.

Their backward-facing barbs anchor the stinger in skin and work it deeper with each stroke. Scorpions and spiders deliver venom differently, by squeezing muscles around a venom gland.

Each lancet carries a small, flexible flap, called a valve, inside the chamber. The two valves move in opposite directions: when one travels down toward the tip, the other travels up.

A single stroke moves a valve about a sixtieth of an inch (0.45 millimeters), roughly the thickness of four sheets of paper, in about seven tenths of a second. The venom then leaves through a canal about half the width of a human hair.

On the downstroke, each valve inflates like a parachute and pushes venom ahead of it. On the upstroke it collapses, so venom can flow past it and refill the chamber below while the other valve is pushing.

The top of the chamber is also wider than the valves can seal, which leaves a space where fresh venom keeps entering even while pumping goes on.

Then the two valves meet. “Finally, and perhaps most dramatically, as the valves meet in the middle of the stroke, they change shape again to push past each other,” said Ramirez-Esquivel.

“This is a remarkable strategy to pump fluid since maintaining a seal is vital to transmit pressure effectively.”

There are no muscles inside the chamber or the valves, so every change of shape is passive.

To test the idea, the team scanned stingers from a Canberra hive at the Australian National University and 3D printed a scaled-up chamber with flexible plastic valves pumping glycerol. Its valves moved like the real ones.

A syringe shows why that matters. Its one rigid piston can’t refill without pulling back, so it can’t deliver a steady flow. The stinger’s two collapsing pistons pump and refill at once.

“The stinger pump design is quite unusual in having two pistons in a single pumping chamber,” Ramirez-Esquivel told Earth.com.

She said that, as manufacturing advances, the design may become practical to produce at scale for uses such as medical pumps for drug delivery.

The stinger has already inspired microneedle designs, and mosquito mouthparts have inspired 3D printing nozzles.

Asked by Earth.com the best way to remove a stinger, Ramirez-Esquivel said the stinger empties the venom sac within about 30 seconds to two minutes.

Taking it out as quickly as possible limits how much venom gets into the skin, she said. Near a hive, though, it is better to get away calmly and quickly first.

The reason is in the stinger itself. It carries glands that release alarm pheromones, chemical signals that recruit other bees to sting. “If there is something worse than getting stung once it is getting stung multiple times,” she said.

The stinger’s independence also makes sense for the bee. A worker that leaves its stinger behind dies, but the stinger keeps delivering venom whether or not the bee survives.

The authors wrote that this suits an insect that defends its colony with its life.

The team could not directly see venom flowing inside the chamber. The refill space at the top is inferred from the shapes and timing of the valves.

Whether the collapsing valve fully stops venom from being sucked back up is also unknown, and the authors wrote that more work is needed to measure that.

How the valves squeeze past each other is unresolved too. The video suggests the cup-shaped part of each valve collapses sideways, while in the printed model the valve’s wings flipped upward. The authors wrote that future work is needed to settle which happens in the real stinger.

In addition, the authors have not measured what the valves are made of, because each one is small and fragile enough to damage on removal. And every stinger was filmed in gel, not living skin.

The next step the authors proposed is to freeze stingers in liquid nitrogen in mid-sting and scan them, catching the valves in whatever shape they take as they pass.

The scans from this study are public on MorphoSource for anyone who wants to look.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

#6339. The Sky Today on Friday, November 6: Nab the North America Nebula

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

As fall gets into full swing, we are seeing less of the summertime stars. By 6 P.M. local time, the Summer Triangle — which flies high overhead on short summer nights — is now starting to set in the west. Lowest of its three points is Vega in Lyra; to Vega’s upper left is Altair in Aquila, while Deneb in Cygnus is almost directly above Vega and the highest of the three.

With no Moon in the sky, let’s use Deneb to find a favorite deep-sky object: NGC 7000, the North America Nebula. It’s a great small scope target, and its location just 3° east of Deneb makes it easy to center in the eyepiece. However, this huge emission nebula stretches about 2° across, so note that it requires a larger field of view to capture all in one go. It definitely benefits from a nebula filter if you have one.

On the sky, the nebula’s western side looks like the eastern coast of the continent for which it is named, and vice versa. The curve that mimics the Gulf of Mexico is particularly prominent, so start there if you’re having trouble seeing the shape. Look also to NGC 7000’s west — across a dark gulf, you’ll see a fainter, more compact patch of nebulosity. This is IC 5067/5070, also known as the Pelican Nebula.

Sunrise: 6:35 A.M.Sunset: 4:52 P.M.Moonrise: 3:56 A.M.Moonset: 3:16 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning crescent (5%)*Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

#6338. The 7 Best Robot Vacuums Withstood Every Mess We Threw at Them

We scattered crumbs, dust, and debris to determine which models could power through these piles of mess without a hiccup.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

If you find cleaning your house to be a drag, robot vacuums do some of the dirty work for you. These intuitive little machines keep your floors tidy by vacuuming up dust, food crumbs, pet hair, and more—all without requiring you to lift a finger. They’re the ultimate “set it and forget it” cleaning solution because with robot vacuums, there’s no longer a need for you to lug around a heavy canister or upright vacuum.

Robot vacuums have come a long way in recent years. Today’s models are smarter, faster, and more capable than ever before. Many have the ability to map your home’s layout, create custom cleaning routines, and empty their own dustbins.

They’re also packed with sophisticated sensors to avoid stairs and furniture, dodge socks and dog toys, and skirt past other obstacles. Some models also include mopping functionality for complete floor care. And app and voice control allow you to start, stop, and schedule your vacuum to run from anywhere.

Below, we’ve gathered some valuable tips on what to look for in a robot vacuum and how to use these devices. Plus, find out how we tested the top robot vacuums and which one is best for you.

For models that we tested in-house, we set up three 8-by-8-foot pens, each with a different floor surface, to simulate various cleaning scenarios for each robot vacuum. One pen featured low- to medium-pile carpet. The second had bare, polished concrete, and the third had laminate flooring. We set a stool, floor mat, and ottoman on the concrete to act as common obstacles found in the home.

In each pen, we also scattered flour, dried rice, and crushed up cereal to represent different types of dirt and detritus. This stress test pushed the vacuums beyond typical maintenance cleaning, so we could assess how they handle more material compared to an average encounter.

To better understand how these robot vacuums functioned in everyday environments, we sent several models home with staff members and testers for real-world experience. This allowed us to confidently evaluate how each device handled household challenges like pet hair, kids’ messes, and varying floor types.

Our testers used the vacuums for a month or more, assessing them based on key criteria like features, cleaning effectiveness, navigation capability, ease of use, and overall value. Although these selections were not subjected to standardized lab testing, our recommendations are grounded in hands-on experience and long-term use.

We are continuously refining this list to reflect the latest advancements in robot technology. Our ongoing updates show our commitment to providing trustworthy, up-to-date guidance and selections that are relevant. As new components are introduced and we test more models, we always carefully evaluate and incorporate these insights to help you choose the right tools for maintaining a clean and comfortable home.

We’ll soon be testing the Roborock QV 35A Robot Vacuum, which is an uprgraded version of our previous Best Overall recommendation, the Qrevo S. The latest model offers much of the same functionality, along with a few improvements—and a couple trade-offs.

Like its predecessor, the QV 35A is a dual system that both vacuums and mops, but it increases suction power up to 8,000 Pascals—1,000 more than the Qrevo S—for stronger cleaning performance. The spinning mop heads reach 200 rotations per minute and lift 10 millimeters, helping prevent carpets and area rugs from getting wet as the robot vacuum moves between thresholds. However, unlike the Qrevo S, the mop heads rely on air drying rather than using a hot air drying system, which could mean longer downtime between cleaning sessions.

Beyond cleaning performance, the QV 35A uses LiDAR navigation to scan and mop your home, creating detailed layouts within the companion app. It stores up to four floor plans, making it a practical option for multi-story households. The app also supports a range of customization features like scheduled cleanings, custom routes. and real-time machine monitoring.

To support all of this, the highly capable docking station is designed for lower maintenance. It holds 2.7 liters of dry debris and 4 liters of water, allowing for several weeks of use before needing attention. Taken all together, these features suggest the QV 35A should perform similarly to the Qrevo S, which handled laminate, concrete, and medium-pile carpet effectively during our previous testing.

If you–or your pet–tend to shed a lot of hair, the Eureka J15 Pro robot vacuum should be your next home cleaning investment. The base has a built-in, automatic hair cutting tool that slices through tangles any time it docks, so you don’t have manually remove hair from the roller.

This robot vacuum isn’t lacking in power, either. It delivers 16,000 Pa suction for a deeper clean, and it works on a variety of floor types like carpet, area rugs, hardwood, linoleum, and tile. The J15 Pro has advanced obstacle detection, and our tester, who has been using this model for months, tells us that it’s great at avoiding furniture, cords, pet toys, and over-friendly pets. It even takes a picture whenever it runs into something in its cleaning path, and you’re able to view the photo within the map afterwards in case it’s something that should be moved liked shoes and cords (or an animal).

The mopping feature is also effective at keeping your house clean. There are two microfiber pads that are spring-loaded to add pressure for a deeper clean, and they extend to get close to walls, corners, and baseboards. Our tester found the J15 Pro to be quiet on all modes, but Turbo is noticeably louder than the nighttime mode. You have control over suction power, though, so it doesn’t have to be running at full capacity constantly if you want to cut down on background noise.

She does mention that while this is a smart device and the app is advanced, it’s a little overwhelming to deal with. There are a plethora of settings and options available, and while it’s easy to set up basic settings initially, it gets a lot more involved. Those who are really just looking for daily maintenance and don’t want all the bells and whistles may find this cumbersome.

As a first-time robot vacuum owner, our tester has been very pleased with his ongoing experience using the dreame X40 Ultra. It’s been able to take on dirt, dust, crumbs, and anything that his dog tracks inside, and exceeded expectations on hardwood floors. There are a few places it struggled to reach, like under a coffee table and TV stand, but we chalk that up to a height issue rather than capability concerns.

The X40 Ultra has 12,000 Pa of suction power, and a liftable, extendable side brush that gets close to wall corners and furniture legs. To protect rugs and carpets from getting wet, the robot vacuum either detaches the mop heads or lifts them to 10.5 millimeters, preventing any wet and dry mess combinations.

The app also allows you to program no-go zones, including rugs or other problem areas like staircases. Even with pet toys laying around the house, the X40 was able to navigate and map the layout with ease, all while avoiding these obstacles.

The mopping feature is a favorite for our tester. If you’re constantly on the go, having a robot vacuum capable of mopping on a daily basis is a real game changer. And thanks to auto-empty and auto-refill tanks, it’s really a set-it-and-forget-it device. We only suggest that you run the robot vacuum overnight so you aren’t disturbed by its run cycle. (Waking up to beautiful, clean floors is fun, too.)

Full Dreame X40 Ultra Robotic Vacuum Review

Ecovacs has been around since the late 90’s, and the brand introduced its first Deebot in 2007. Needless to say, its designs have come along way, and one of the latest versions piqued our interest for one main reason: stain removal.

Most often, robot vacuums with mopping capability can only handle fresh spills on hardwood and tile, not the stubborn, dried-on stuff. The Deebot X12 is trying to change that. It uses an AI camera and infrared stain detector to identify spills, splatters, and even muddy paw prints. Then, it deploys two jets with cleaning solution at up to 46,000 Pascals to loosen residue for the mop roller head to pick up. This could potentially save you from having to make a more detailed pass by hand.

The vacuum has capable power on carpet, too. It uses 22,000 Pascals of suction power to get rid or dirt, hair, and debris, and features an anti-tangle side and main brush to prevent hair from getting trapped around the bristles and roller.

The docking station is one of the more advanced designs we’ve seen in a robot vacuum. It has a bagless dustbin, power washing for the mop roller, and hot air drying. We’re looking forward to testing out this model and updating this guide accordingly with our findings.

Full Ecovacs Deebot X12 Omnicycle Robot Vacuum and Mop Review

The Qrevo CurvX is a newer design from Roborock, and we like that is has a slimmer build to fit under a wider variety of furniture, but still packs 22,000 Pa of suction power (the highest on our list). It’s equipped with a range of smart features, including pet recognition technology and two-way video calling (in the Roborock app) to interact with furry friends while you’re away, making it a great choice for households with animals.

The initial mapping process took a bit of time, but alas, this is a crucial step for an accurate layout of your home. Once the mapping was complete, the CurvX navigated efficiently, avoiding unnecessary paths and cleaning strategically as it went. During operation, the vacuum ran very quietly, especially when compared to other Roborock models we’ve experienced.

One of the biggest conveniences is the automatic dustbin emptying system, as it significantly reduces the need for manual maintenance. The tanks hold debris for up to seven weeks, and the water tank automatically refills the reservoir on the robot vacuum so you don’t have to.

The mop lifting and carpet detection performed well in our lab tests. When used in the concrete floor pen with obstacles like a small rug, it raised the heads with ease when transitioning between floor types. This ensured that carpets didn’t get wet during mopping sessions and the robot maintained the right cleaning mode. The edge mopping system is also a fantastic feature. The mop heads sit on arms that extend outwards for better reach, and they were able to get under and around table legs more efficiently.

That being said, this model isn’t without its limitations. In some of our mess tests, it missed detritus that was close to the pen walls, or “room edges,” despite the side brush kicking up the debris. It got closer than other robot vacuums we tested, but this is still a common struggle for many other models.

Full Roborock Qrevo CruvX Robot Vacuum and Mop Review

If you don’t need a robot vacuum with mopping capability, then the Shark PowerDetect is a viable option. It doesn’t sacrifice on features where you need them, and works well on different types of flooring.

Our tester found that the robot vacuum could clean various floor types and pick up after pets with ease. After after just one cycle, they noticed the difference.

The vacuum has one side brush, but since it rotates 360-degrees, it’s able to get close to baseboards and edges without leaving much of anything behind. The PowerDetect also does a great job of moving around obstacles. During testing, the vacuum got pretty close to a hair dryer cord to clean as much of the floor/carpet as possible, but it never tried to vacuum over it or got tangled.

Battery life held up too, and the robot vacuum was able to clean multiple rooms before returning to the docking station to charge. Our tester did note that the battery drains faster in Matrix Clean mode, but this isn’t completely unexpected because max suction requires more power.

One of the first things that sets the Eufy Omni S2 is its unique docking station. Most robot vacuums on the market have tanks that are side by side and sit lower to the ground, but the S2’s docking station is taller and more narrow, making it easier to access to refill and empty (and find a place to store).

Another is suction power. The Omni S2 pulls at up to 30,000 Pa, and our tester noticed the difference immediately, especially in high-traffic spots that get flattened and dull over time. The 100 air watts of consistent airflow was able to pull in dirt, allergens, and pet hair from deep between carpet fibers instead of just picking up debris from the surface.

The S2 uses a DuoSpiral main brush, which is actually two separate brush rolls with a gap in the middle to funnel hair into the suction port to prevent tangles, and it has proven reliable in a household with six pets.

Most mopping robot vacuums use spinning mop heads to clean your floors, but the Omni S2 uses a rolling mop with electrolyzed water and plenty of downward pressure for an even clean. The main downside is there is no option for mopping-only or vacuum-then-mopping cleaning modes. Many of our other recommendations are able to do these processes separately, so it’s definitely something to consider. The base station takes care of much of the dirty maintenance work, including self-emptying, self-refilling, hot water washing and hot air drying of the mop roller.

Full Eufy Omni S2 Robot Vacuum and Mop Review

Many robot vacuums overlap in features and capability, and there are newer and better models releasing all the time. As a result, we’re often adding and swapping out our recommendations in this list. Here are a few other robot vacuums we’ve tested that still warrant recognition:

Eufy X10 Pro Omni Robot Vacuum and Mop: This combination robot vacuum and mop reduces monotonous upkeep tasks with carefully curated features. The docking station lasts for up to 60 days before needing attention, and other key highlights include auto-refill, auto-wash, self-dry, and self-emptying to make maintenance virtually hands-free.

Roborock Curv Flow 2 Robot Vacuum and Mop: The Roborock CurvX we recommend above is the stronger all-around robot vacuum, but the Curv Flow 2 is a good alternative if you want a mop roller that continuously refreshes itself with clean water to prevent dirty mop drag. This robot vacuum is also rated for up to 20,000Pa of suction power, has a larger dustbin, and performs well on hard floors.

Navigation is key to how well a robot vacuum performs its job. Suction matters little if the vacuum fails to cover every part of your floor. Just about all models utilize three fundamental types of sensors to help them navigate.

This navigation method involves a laser that locates features by sending out pulses of light and measuring how long they take to return. LiDAR is especially useful for creating accurate maps and is the most powerful and most common navigation tool for robot vacuums.

With this navigation style, the vacuum travels in one direction and then changes course when it hits an object. A lot of models are programmed to optimize their paths and make them more efficient. By running into a wall in a couple of places, the robot vac can verify the location of the wall and move parallel to it, turning 180 degrees each time they hit an end wall.

Visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (vSLAM)

This triangulates position by tracking multiple points in a room in successive camera frames. Over time, the vacuum learns and becomes more efficient by relying on points that remain constant and do not change.

Suction power, which indicates how strongly a vacuum pulls in air and debris, is typically listed by the manufacturer in pascals (Pa). The bulk of modern vacuums offer anywhere from 4,000 to 10,000 Pa, but with each new model that comes out, we’re seeing those numbers continue to rise, with some upwards of 20,000 Pa. Just be aware that higher suction impacts a robot vacuum’s battery life and noise levels.

A brand’s claims about suction power may not provide the full picture, either. Manufacturers don’t tell us exactly where or how they’re measuring—they may take measurements at the impeller or without passing the filter, or using the vacuum only in a controlled environment. It’s similar to how automakers disclose horsepower ratings on cars as an engine spec. The transmission, differential, and other components all leech some of that horsepower, so what’s actually available at the rear wheels differs from the number listed in the specs.

A large dustbin and water tank capacity are ideal for big homes or households with pets, since they reduce how often you need to empty or refill. For smaller spaces or light daily cleaning, a more compact unit with a capacity of 2 liters should still get the job done. For models that also mop, a clean and dirty water tank of 4 liters or more combined is sufficient for cleaning larger areas efficiently without constant refilling. The models on our list hold between 2.5 and 5.3 liters of debris.

Beyond navigation and suction power, today’s robot vacuums come packed with bells and whistles that elevate them beyond the basic models of the past. Room mapping, self-emptying dustbins, voice assistant compatibility, cleaning schedules, and no-go zones have all become more or less the standard.

The most tech-forward robot vacuums offer AI-powered obstacle recognition that identifies and steers clear of pet waste, shoes, or cables. There are also variations that have dual functionality, combining both vacuum and mopping qualities. As you might expect, the more advanced sensors and assets a robot vacuum offers, the higher its price tag.

Throughout our testing process, we discovered that while the mopping features are certainly useful, they don’t fully deliver the type of power or pressure needed to get rid of tough stains or set-in messes. The docking stations are also made for water only, and it’s not recommended to use any kind of detergents or DIY solutions in the robot. Some brands make their own cleaners that you can purchase separately, but make sure its compatible with your specific model. If you’re dealing with really stubborn grime, we recommend keeping a standard mop on hand.

Look out for shoelaces, string, carpet fringe, and thin or lightweight clothing—all of which gets easily caught in brushes and rollers. Some units have sensors that stop them when the brushes meet resistance, and some move in reverse, spitting out whatever they pulled in. This technology isn’t foolproof, so it’s best to just keep the area clear.

Additionally, be aware of pet bowls, plant stands, or other things that could tip over until you know how the robot vacuum interacts with them. Models that leverage bump-and-go navigation may knock things a little harder, so it’s a good idea to set up boundaries to avoid those obstacles.

Lastly, if you have kids, many robot vacuums are capable of picking up small toys (or parts of toys) that are strewn about. A lot of units have the ability to create exclusion zones, so make use of them, or employ your own strategy to avoid all these little hazards that could jam up the vacuum.

Most homes have places where a robot won’t reach, like in between narrowly spaced furniture legs or tight corners. Also, some types of dirt and debris overwhelm robot vacuum filters, since their capacities are pretty small. Fine dust, fireplace ash, and powders, even in moderate quantities, could clog a filter and affect performance.

When set on a consistent schedule, robot vacuums help your house look clean on a day-to-day basis. Still, it’s best to run your upright or cordless stick vacuum for deeper cleans and bigger messes.

Place the robot vacuum and docking station in an open space that’s close to a power outlet. The power connection is essential for charging the vacuum and running automatic dustbin emptying features. When the space in front of the docking station is open and obstacle-free, the vacuum is able to tackle dirt more frequently. Try to avoid putting the unit near high-pile carpeting, near stairs, or cluttered spaces.

For homes with high foot traffic, pets, or children, running your vacuum on a daily basis is ideal. Three to four times a week is best for homes with moderate foot traffic, and if you live in an apartment, or your home has multiple spare rooms that don’t get used very often, running your robot vacuum weekly (or simply as needed) will suffice.

Most units have physical controls on the vacuum to start, stop, and send the vacuum back to the docking station. However, smart features like app control, scheduling, mapping, and voice assistants require internet connection. We recommend connecting the vacuum to your home network to get the most out of these features.

About half of people with long COVID see meaningful improvement in their symptoms after three years, a new study found.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Symptoms of long COVID ease in half of patients within three years of the infection that kicked off their illness.

That's the primary conclusion of a new study that tracked over 1,000 patients with long COVID, a chronic condition that can emerge after an infection with the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Among the patients, the chance of improvement varied sharply depending on how the condition affected their bodily systems.

In the study, published Tuesday (Nov. 3) in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine, roughly 60% of patients whose predominant symptoms were changes to their ability to taste or smell had significantly improved three years after their first positive test. But less than 20% of those with a multisystem presentation had improved in that time frame.

This latter group had symptoms that affected their cardiac, nervous and gastrointestinal systems, among others. An expert told Live Science that the condition resembled myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), which often arises after an infection and similarly impacts a wide range of bodily systems.

The new study's findings could help direct the structure of future clinical trials of treatments for long COVID, experts said.

The patients in the study were enrolled in the long-term RECOVER Adult Study. Funded by the National Institutes of Health, the project has recruited thousands of adults across the United States who previously tested positive for COVID-19.

Researchers scored patients based on how they were affected by a range of symptoms, including fatigue, brain fog, shortness of breath and heart palpitations. The study included patients who scored more than 10 points on a 30-point scale — called the 2024 LC Research Index (LCRI) — which attempted to capture these different symptom combinations.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Nearly 1,020 patients met this requirement and were tracked over time; they had in-person appointments and filled out symptom surveys every three months. Scientists marked patients as "improved" once they recorded LCRI scores of 10 or less at two consecutive visits. They found that 36% of the participants had improved two years after their inciting COVID-19 infection, and that figure rose to 50% after three years.

LCRIs hit zero for 26% of the participants after three years, meaning all of their symptoms were gone at the time of the survey.

Reeder said he was careful to avoid describing the participants as "recovered." This decision was influenced by input from the long COVID community to the RECOVER Adult Study, he said. They highlighted that their symptoms can wax and wane, whereas "recovery" implies a permanent resolution. The new study didn't capture, for example, whether individual patients who recorded meaningful improvement later relapsed.

The researchers analyzed which SARS-CoV-2 strain was associated with the most long COVID cases, controlling for patient vaccination status.

Some patients' journeys were far less straightforward than the top-line data might suggest. Although men and women improved at similar rates, adults under 46 were more likely to improve than older participants were. Patients affected by the Omicron variants of SARS-CoV-2, which emerged in 2021 and quickly became the dominant strain of the virus, were more likely to improve than those infected with earlier strains.

Some of the starkest differences in improvement rates were seen between patients with different symptoms.

In a previous study, RECOVER researchers had grouped participants into five subtypes, using an algorithm to connect patients with similar predominant symptoms:

In the new study, patients in the last three groups were less likely to get better within three years. The final group's rate was particularly low, at just 19%.

Dr. Carmen Scheibenbogen, an immunologist at Charité University Medicine Berlin, said these patients' progress resembles that of people with ME/CFS.

"It looks as if at least a major subgroup is suffering from ME-CFS," Scheibenbogen said, noting that COVID-19 may have triggered their condition. "This is a disease which is triggered by different infections, but in the end, the disease [itself] is very similar," she said.

Like long COVID, ME/CFS can affect a wide array of bodily systems, and it remains poorly understood despite recent advances in research.

The team's new findings highlight the need for clinical trials to test possible treatments for long COVID. Both Scheibenbogen and study co-author Harrison Reeder, a biostatistician at Massachusetts General Hospital, said these subtypes would be important to consider in the design of these potential trials.

The multisystem subgroup, Reeder said, "might be a group where an effective intervention can make a bigger difference than people who stand to potentially have a higher chance of improvement regardless."

Future work would need to further scientists' understanding of people affected by long COVID at the level of their genes and proteins, both scientists said.

"There's a lot of work to do in RECOVER and in the world of long COVID research," Harrison said. "There's a lot of opportunity."

#6336. When eco-friendly advertising backfires: More green claims can make a product less appealing

Advertising both eco-friendly ingredients and sustainable packaging can lower a product’s appeal among shoppers who care less about buying green.

A product made with eco-friendly ingredients and sold in sustainable packaging sounds like an easy sell.

But a new study suggests that advertising both benefits can make it less appealing to some shoppers.

People who care a lot about buying green rated a product higher when its ad mentioned both. People who care less rated it higher when the ad stuck to just one.

At least with these ads, more green information wasn’t automatically more persuasive.

Miyuri Shirai, a professor at Keio University, tested this in three experiments with 1,729 people in Japan. The products were made up for the study, and people rated ads instead of buying anything.

Soap, cereal, detergent and other things people buy over and over are called consumer packaged goods. A growing number of them are sold as better for the planet.

In 2023, 18.5% of these goods sold in the US were marketed as sustainable, according to the NYU Stern Center for Sustainable Business. That’s up 4.8 percentage points from 2015.

McKinsey & Company and NielsenIQ found that products with sustainability claims grew their sales by 28% over five years, compared with 20% for products without those claims.

Growth like that leaves companies with a choice. They can make the product itself greener by changing what goes into it or how it’s made. Or they can work on the packaging, using better materials, a new design or a package that can be recycled.

Sustainable packaging gets a lot of attention because these products are bought and thrown away so often. All that packaging uses up raw materials and energy and adds to pollution.

Doing both often costs more and makes production harder. So it helps to know whether shoppers actually reward the extra effort.

At first glance, two green features should beat one. Researchers call this the more-is-better pattern, where the more good things an ad says about a product, the better people tend to rate it.

A much older finding suggests otherwise. In a 1992 study, Daniel Kahneman and Jack Knetsch looked at how much people were willing to pay for environmental services.

People tended to value something less when it came as part of a bigger package than when it was judged on its own. This is called the embedding effect, and it’s where Shirai’s question started.

“My interest in this research began when I read articles about the embedding effect, which suggest that adding more positive information does not always make an option seem better,” Shirai said.

“I became curious about whether communicating multiple sustainability benefits might sometimes be less effective than highlighting just one, depending on the consumer,” she added.

At Keio’s Faculty of Business and Commerce, Shirai studies the psychology of how shoppers judge products. For this project, she recruited people through Freeasy, a Japanese online survey panel.

Each person saw one ad for a made-up product. Some ads talked only about what the product was made of, others only about the packaging, and the rest about both.

People then rated the product. Shirai also measured how much each person cares about buying things that are good for the environment, which researchers call green consumption values.

The first experiment used laundry detergent. Of the 750 people recruited, 124 failed a check meant to catch careless answers, which left 626.

The second used organic granola, a food that’s widely sold and already seen as sustainable.

Switching from detergent to food helped test whether the pattern held across different product categories.

This time, 600 of the 750 recruits made it through the same check.

Body wash was the product in the third experiment, which included 503 people. Those people also answered extra questions to help explain why they reacted the way they did.

In all three experiments, the results came out the same way.

People who cared more about green buying rated the product higher when the ad covered both the product and its packaging than when it covered only one.

People who cared less did the reverse. They rated the product higher when the ad stuck to a single feature.

That second group’s response was consistent with the embedding effect.

For them, one green feature may have seemed less impressive when it came bundled with another.

For the first group, Shirai had a different explanation. It’s hard to tell how green a product really is from an ad or a label, so people look for small clues.

For someone who cares a lot about the environment, details about the product and details about its package may work as two clues that back each other up.

“Emphasizing sustainability in both the product and its packaging may not always be the most effective strategy,” she said.

In the body wash experiment, people also rated how useful they found the green information and how sustainable they thought the product was.

Both ratings were linked to how people felt about the product, and those links depended on each person’s green values.

The analysis couldn’t show which came first, though, so this is a possible explanation rather than proof.

There’s one catch in how the ads were built.

The ads that mentioned both the product and its packaging had four green statements, while the single-focus ads had two each.

So the results can’t show for sure what people were reacting to. It could have been the number of claims, or whether the claims covered one feature or two.

Everyone in the study was in Japan, and participants rated fictional products without spending real money.

Whether tailoring ads to shoppers’ green values would increase sales or benefit the environment remains untested.

The full study was published in the Journal of Environmental Psychology.

#6335. Nov. 6, 1919: Einstein is right

The earliest test of Albert Einstein’s general theory of relativity took place just four years after he published it. During the May 29, 1919, total solar eclipse, British astronomer Sir Arthur Eddington and colleagues studied the theory by measuring how the Sun distorts light from background stars.

According to general relativity, any object with mass warps space-time. (The common analogy is that it’s similar to a bowling ball on a trampoline.) So, any passing body will follow a curved trajectory; this is true whether the passing body is an orbiting satellite or a light photon from a background object.

Researchers involved with the 1919 eclipse expedition traveled to two locations to observe totality: northern Brazil and a western island of Africa. According to general relativity, the apparent positions of stars near the Sun would appear to shift by 1.75 arcseconds. The scientists first measured the positions of stars in the Hydra star cluster in early 1919. Eddington and colleagues then recorded the stars’ locations during totality, and compared them to the previous values. They found that indeed, the background stars appeared to shift by roughly the amount general relativity had predicted. (They measured 1.98 arcseconds and 1.61 arcseconds.) The researchers announced their data on Nov. 6, 1919, and Einstein quickly became a household name.

Liz Kruesi is science writer with a background in physics who specializes in astronomy and space-related news.

#6334. Little Ice Age cooling in Europe may have raised the risk of rickets

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Skeletal remains with signs of vitamin D deficiencies hint at how climate change impacted health

A volcano-fueled chilly climate during the 18th and 19th centuries may have made winter in England so bad, as depicted in this 19th century painting of a man collecting wood, that it raised the risk of kids getting rickets, a condition caused by vitamin D deficiency.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

England isn’t renowned for its weather. But just a few centuries ago, climate change–fueled conditions may have been so bad that they put children’s health at risk.

Calcium mineralization in the teeth and skeletons of people who lived in rural northern England suggests that children growing up during the height of the Little Ice Age routinely developed vitamin D deficiencies, researchers report November 5 in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. In the worst cases, these deficiencies developed into rickets, a bone disorder that can occur when people don’t get enough ultraviolet light.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Previous skeletal studies suggest that rickets became more common among Europeans during the 18th and 19th centuries. One culprit may have been the Industrial Revolution, when many Europeans lived in UV-poor polluted cities and often worked indoors. The unusually cold climate may have added “an extra layer of difficulty” to getting enough sunlight, says Ellen Kendall, a bioarcheologist at Durham University in England

The Little Ice Age was a period of global cooling from the 13th to 19th centuries caused by extreme solar cycles and a series of volcanic eruptions, which can cool the planet by ejecting aerosols into the atmosphere that block sunlight. In the last 200 years of the era, 18 major eruptions helped spur a temperature drop of 2 to 3 degrees Celsius over northern Europe.

Kendall and colleagues wondered how this cold climate affected health. They examined calcium deposition — how the essential mineral is incorporated into bones — in the remains of 21 people buried from 1711 to 1829 in the town of North Shields. Calcium often doesn’t fully mineralize in people with vitamin D delicacies, leaving voids in teeth as they grow.

The team found bands of failed calcium mineralization in the teeth, suggesting seasonal spates of vitamin D deficiencies. Some skeletons also showed signs of rickets. North Shields was a small rural town that hadn’t yet undergone industrialization, so these deficiencies probably weren’t due to bad air conditions.

The unusually cold weather may have changed people’s behavior during the winter, Kendall says. Residents may have kept their kids indoors or bundled them up so that little skin was exposed when they did go outside, preventing them from getting enough UV light, she says.

However, climate was still just one factor among many — including gender roles, diet and pollution — that shaped vitamin D deficiencies at the time, says Kendall. “Humans are very messy to study,” she says. “That’s one of the things that makes them so very fascinating.”

#6333. Construction crews in California accidentally unearthed the bones of a large mammal that lived 40 to 45 million years ago

Fossils found during construction in Oceanside, California, may belong to a giant hoofed mammal that lived 40 to 45 million years ago.

During routine excavation for a city infrastructure project in Oceanside, California, Joseph El Adli, a principal paleontologist with Helix Environmental Planning, spotted fossil bones about 12 feet (3.7 meters) below the surface. He recognized their importance and secured the area.

The bones belong to a large, hoofed mammal that lived 40 to 45 million years ago, the City of Oceanside announced on September 22, 2026.

The animal may be a titanothere, nicknamed “thunder beast,” or Amynodon, historically called a “swamp rhino.” Laboratory work should settle which.

He was monitoring the dig as the project’s paleontologist. The city places monitors on major infrastructure work as standard practice and to comply with California environmental laws.

The find includes several limb bones, ribs and numerous other bones and fragments. The largest piece appears to be a femur.

El Adli’s team worked for seven days to expose the bones from beneath several tons of hardened mudstone and sandstone.

The fossils were then wrapped in a plaster field jacket and moved to an off-site laboratory.

The exact location has not been disclosed, to protect public safety and the integrity of the site.

The bones came from Member C of the Santiago Formation, a thick sequence of sedimentary rock in northwestern San Diego County.

Paleontologists based the age estimate on the known age of that rock and the types of organisms found in it. The range falls within the Eocene Epoch, in a stretch of time called the Uintan North American Land Mammal Age.

According to the city, the animal roamed ancient floodplains in the area.

The same rock unit in the city has yielded Diegoaelurus vanvalkenburghae, a predator named in a 2022 description of Diegoaelurus. It belongs to the machaeroidines, the oldest group of sabertooth mammals.

Known from a nearly complete lower jaw with most of its teeth, it is the youngest machaeroidine on record. Its authors tentatively tie the group’s extinction to faunal change at the shift from the middle to the late Eocene, part of a wider turnover among mammal predators.

The fossil site that produced it, known as Jeff’s Discovery, also holds a tapir relative called Hesperaletes and a hyaenodontid predator, Limnocyon.

The paper was led by Shawn Zack of the University of Arizona College of Medicine in Phoenix, with Ashley Poust of the San Diego Natural History Museum.

Both candidates belong to Perissodactyla, the order of odd-toed hoofed mammals that includes today’s horses, rhinos and tapirs. Titanotheres are also known as brontotheres.

Oceanside officials describe them as animals roughly the size of a black rhino, with deep chests, a distinct shoulder hump and small horns.

In 2001, paleontologists collected brontothere remains from a sandstone layer at another construction site in Oceanside, near Rancho del Oro Road.

That animal, Parvicornus, stood about 5 to 6 feet (1.5 to 1.8 meters) at the shoulder, according to the San Diego Natural History Museum. It had only a very small horn, more of a bump, near each eye.

Brontotheres began as dog-size animals in the early Eocene and grew larger over roughly 20 million years. Those in South Dakota’s Badlands, about 38 to 34 million years ago, reached around 8 feet (2.4 meters) tall and 16 feet (4.9 meters) long.

The Badlands animals carried blunt, paired horns on their noses, sometimes more than 3.3 feet (1 meter) long. Males had larger horns than females.

These herbivores most likely ate soft leaves in Eocene forests. The group died out at the end of the Eocene, likely as the climate turned cooler and drier, the National Park Service notes.

Amynodon is the namesake of the amynodonts, which the American Museum of Natural History describes as large-bodied, hornless rhinos. Amynodon itself had a squat, hippo-like body, city officials say.

Their nickname comes from an older idea that they spent much of their time in water. Evidence for that is very limited.

Only Metamynodon, the last North American amynodont, may have been semi-aquatic. Its fossils turn up in sandstone laid down by rivers.

Amynodonts lived in Asia and North America from the middle Eocene through the early Oligocene. They have no living relatives and sit far from today’s species on the rhino family tree.

Amynodon had a large hollow in the skull in front of each eye socket. It likely anchored muscles for an enlarged upper lip.

At the laboratory, preparators will remove the plaster jackets. They will then harden and stabilize the fossils with museum-grade glues and resins.

Once the bones are fully freed from the surrounding rock, paleontologists expect to narrow down the animal’s precise identity.

The specimens are expected to join a museum collection, where they will be preserved and available to scientists and the public. The museum has not been named.

Several jacketed blocks have not been opened yet, and a skull may be inside one of them.

The information was obtained from the City of Oceanside.

#6331. The Sky Today on Saturday, November 7: Venus meets the Moon

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Venus is already primed to capture attention above the eastern horizon before sunrise. This morning, the Moon passes 1.1° due south of Earth’s sister planet at 7 A.M. EST.

You can easily catch the pair an hour before sunrise, some 6° high in the east and climbing as the sky begins to brighten. Magnitude –4.5 Venus blazes to the upper left of the delicate crescent Moon, whose western limb is just barely lit as the Sun sets across the lunar nearside. Look for earthshine on the already-shadowed portion of Luna’s face, as sunlight bouncing off Earth lights it up.

Near Venus is another bright light: This is Spica, Virgo’s alpha star, shining at magnitude 1.0 and also lingering in the morning twilight. This morning it lies 1.3° northeast of Venus, with the planet and star roughly side by side above the horizon. Use this view as an anchor point: By the 10th, Venus will have moved to stand due west of this star and will be located to its upper right.

Live Science readers respond to a recent poll about whether they'd visit the Red Planet even with potential health risks.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For centuries, Mars has been seen as a potential place for future human settlements. But long-duration space travel comes with serious risks to astronauts' health, including those resulting from cosmic radiation and the effects of microgravity.

A new study found that rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what astronauts might encounter during a Mars mission developed more scar tissue around their hearts' small blood vessels compared with a control group. Although the findings haven't been validated in humans, the results contribute to growing concerns about the potential effects of long-haul space missions on astronauts' health.

Given these new findings, Live Science asked its readers whether they'd travel to the Red Planet, despite these potential health risks. Over 240 readers weighed in, with 65% picking "No, I don't think the risks are worth it."

Interestingly enough, the comments reflect a slightly different trend. One reader wrote, "Any pioneers who travel to Mars will be facing the prospect of death and never coming back. Even if they make it back, there are any number of health issues that could come up. These risks have not stopped people from exploring throughout human history. The bigger question is who to send?"

Other commenters echoed this sentiment, with another reader posting, "Explorers in the past have always been exposed to unusual risks; without the risk takers we would still believe the world is flat."

Beyond the feelings that Mars will be explored anyway, despite the health risks, other commenters highlighted the cost of these missions, with one reader stating, "Sending flesh water balloons to Mars is ridiculous. For the cost of one human on Mars, we could literally probe the entire solar system and map/sample/rove every planet and every major Moon."

Others highlighted the mental and emotional cost of a trip to Mars. "As a devoted sci-fi fan for decades, I always wished I could go into space," another reader noted. "Now that I am 77 years old, I realize I would miss the outdoors. The wind and trees, the birdsong and sweet grass under my feet would be a devastating loss. Let the brave explorers go instead. Life is too brief to leave this planet for the uncertainty and dangers of space travel."

Do you agree with these readers? Let us know your thoughts in the comments!

#6328. Nov. 7, 1882: A Great Comet transforms astrophotography

In early September 1882, a comet was sighted from the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa. The comet brightened over the following weeks, reaching a magnitude of -2 on the 15th; at perihelion two days later, it was bright enough to be visible during the day. But at the time, David Gill, the director of the Cape Observatory, was busy observing minor planets Victoria and Sappho. It wasn’t until Oct. 12 that, his minor planet observations completed, he turned his attention to the comet and began photographing it.

Gill captured images of the Great Comet of 1882 on Oct. 12, 20, and 21, and Nov. 7, 13, and 14. The Nov. 7 shot was the one he would become famous for, though: It was not the first photograph of a comet, but rather would signal a change in astronomers’ uses of astrophotography. The photo was a 100-minute exposure, resulting an image that included stars to 10th magnitude and the comet’s 18-degree tail. Spurred by the large number of stars captured in his photo, Gill saw the potential for using astrophotography for star mapping and began the Cape Photographic Durchmusterung. (Durchmusterung means “close examination” or “scrutiny.”) The project would catalog nearly a half-million southern stars. Gill shared the successes of the program internationally, prompting the assembly of the world’s first major astronomical conference. As a result, astronomers worldwide began to move away from traditional, manual star mapping and towards more efficient and comprehensive photographic techniques.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

#6327. Record-low temperature created on China’s space station

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A Bose-Einstein condensate reached about 10 trillionths of a kelvin

An experiment on China's Tiangong space station (rendering shown) reached a record-low temperature in a state of matter called a Bose-Einstein condensate.

Shujianyang/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Science has reached a new low. Temperature, that is.

Scientists cooled a collection of atoms to about 10 picokelvins, or 10 trillionths of a kelvin. That’s barely a smidge above absolute zero (−273.15° Celsius). The atoms formed a Bose-Einstein condensate, a quantum state of matter, colder than any before, researchers report November 5 in Science.

To achieve that record-low chill, scientists took their work to space. The atoms orbited Earth aboard China’s Tiangong space station. There, researchers used laser-based traps to contain 20,000 rubidium atoms and reduce their motion, thereby cooling them. At an atomic level, temperature is tied to motion: Atoms and molecules in the air around us move more slowly when it’s colder. Similarly, in systems of cold atoms, scientists can define an effective temperature based on how slowly the atoms spread apart when they are allowed to expand.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

On Earth, gravitational forces cause clouds of atoms to sag, reducing the effectiveness of cooling. But on the space station, the atoms experienced microgravity, the apparent weightlessness of an object in free fall.

To make a Bose-Einstein condensate, a disorderly gaggle of atoms is cooled until the atoms all take on the same quantum state, acting as one entity. By experimenting with ultracold atoms, researchers can study exotic states of matter and other mysterious physics. And they can test fundamental concepts, such as the equivalence principle — the idea that explains why objects of different masses fall at the same rate in a vacuum.

Spacefaring Bose-Einstein condensates were previously made on the International Space Station, at effective temperatures as low as 52 picokelvins. And an experiment on Earth, in which atoms were dropped down a tower to induce weightlessness, reached 38 picokelvins. But drop tower experiments are limited by the time their free fall lasts. That’s not an issue for experiments in Earth’s orbit. So cold atoms in space are really taking off.

The surest way to get a scratch from a feline is to go for a forbidden tummy rub. But why do cats hate being touched on their bellies?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Dogs typically love belly rubs and will roll on their backs to get more. With cats, it's a different story: Most are visibly uncomfortable when someone touches their belly, and the same applies to their feet and tail.

When a cat is petted in these areas, its body language often changes. "They might do a quick head turn, looking at your hand, or they might start moving away from you or wiggling around a lot, basically trying to get away from the petting," Mikel Delgado, a cat behaviorist and senior research scientist at Purdue University, told Live Science in an email. "If these early warning signs are ignored, they might escalate to biting, hissing or scratching."

But why do cats dislike it so much when humans touch these specific areas?

Although there has been little formal research into this question, animal behavior experts proposed a few ideas for why cats don't like to be touched in certain areas.

"Cats are prey animals as well as predators and so they can be very protective of areas that are particularly vulnerable to injury during attack, such as the belly area," Sarah Ellis, head of cat mental well-being and behavior at the cat welfare charity International Cat Care, told Live Science in an email.

A cat's belly houses vital organs ‪—‬ such as the liver, stomach and intestines ‪—‬ without the protective bony cage that the ribs provide for the heart and lungs. Although cats have evolved a special feature called the "primordial pouch" —‬ basically a flap of loose skin and fat on their belly —‬ which provides a little extra padding to protect vital organs during fights, most cats still feel threatened when humans touch or rub their belly.

Cats have extra padding on their stomachs to protect their organs.

Dogs have a similar anatomy to cats, but they have to worry less about falling prey to larger animals. Cats, meanwhile, can be hunted by dogs, urban coyotes, and even birds such as hawks and owls, making it natural for them to be protective of their bellies.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

The tail is also a vulnerable area for cats. "When a cat is chased by another animal, including other cats, the tail is often the part of the cat's body that is closest to touch," Ellis said, "and the risk of being bitten at the base of the tail is high." Therefore, cats may be skittish about having their tail stroked.

When it comes to foot rubs, there are two possible explanations for why most cats hate them. First, a cat's paws are essential in threatening situations. Running away from danger is a cat's preferred survival strategy, and they rely on their paws as a means of escape, Ellis explained. If they can't run away, "a cat may resort to repelling any threats through swiping and scratching and it needs its paws free to do so," she said. "It is therefore predisposed to not enjoy having its paws restricted in any way."

Another reason could be that cats' paws are very sensitive. They have wrist whiskers (also known as "carpal vibrissae") and toe pads that are sensitive to various types of stimuli, like pressure and heat, Delgado said, "so it's not surprising that many cats are sensitive about having their feet touched."

If you're interacting with a cat, it's generally a good idea to stick to the areas where most cats like to be petted: the base of their ears, around their cheeks and under their chin. These areas are rich in scent glands, and cats tend to rub them against other cats they are friends with, Delgado explained. So essentially, cats like being petted in those areas because "they treat us as they do other cats," Delgado said.

But some cats go against the grain. "I've had a few who enjoyed belly rubs," Delgado said. Others enjoy having their tail stroked briefly and show their pleasure "by pushing their rump into the hand of the petter and holding their tail up in the air," Ellis said. (This behavior is sometimes called "elevator butt.")

As puzzling as it may be to humans, these varied preferences are a reminder that "each cat is an individual," Delgado said. Positive responses to petting of the belly, feet or tail can also signal close bonding to a human, Ellis said.

She advises people to "always take the cat's lead, learn what each individual cat likes and dislikes and respect these preferences."

#6324. The Sky Today on Sunday, November 8: Io and Callisto race across Jupiter

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Rising with the stars of western Leo shortly before midnight, bright Jupiter and its Galilean moons put on a show early this morning, better visible the farther east you’re located.

Jupiter is just under 5° northwest (to the upper right) of Regulus as they rise in the east. Fainter Mars stands roughly 3° above Jupiter. You’ll want your telescope trained on the gas giant soon after rising to catch the show, which begins at 1:29 A.M. EST as a shadow appears on the planet’s eastern limb. This is Io’s shadow — but don’t be fooled by the positions of the moons you see in your scope. The moon closest to Jupiter on the east is Callisto, while the moon just east of that is Io, whose shadow we see. Ganymede lies farthest east, while Europa is currently hidden behind the planet in an occultation. The latter appears from behind the eastern limb about 1:54 A.M. EST, not long before Callisto reaches the planet and begins a transit at 2:07 A.M. EST.

Keep an eye on Io and Europa: Io passes north of Europa at 2:23 A.M. EST, then heads into its own transit about 2:42 A.M. EST. Now the race is on, as Io approaches and then catches up with Callisto as the two moons transit, passing Callisto and moving west of it within half an hour. The two moons and Io’s shadow continue to transit until 3:45 A.M. EST, when Io’s shadow leaves the western limb, and Io takes about an hour and a quarter longer before egress. Callisto continues trundling along, finally finishing its transit about 5:51 A.M. CST, with the sky now starting to brighten with twilight in the Midwest.

#6323. Nov. 8, 1656: The birth of Edmond Halley

It’s been said that the general public knows three astronomical objects: the Moon, the rings of Saturn, and Halley’s Comet. English astronomer Edmond Halley, born Nov. 8, 1656, didn’t discover the object named for him. In fact, he never even saw it — but his mathematical prediction of its return in 1758 guaranteed his place in history.

Halley was a friend of Isaac Newton and used Newton’s theory of gravity and to calculate “his” comet’s orbit. In fact, Halley published at his own expense the book Newton wrote explaining the theory, Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica. In 1676, Halley sailed to the island of St. Helena in the South Atlantic Ocean and spent a year measuring stellar positions, the result of which was the first catalog of the southern sky.
